hook: The Budapest prodigy who founded game theory, helped build the atomic bomb and designed the modern computer.

pages.x: Neumann János was born in Budapest in 1903, the eldest son of a rich Jewish banker. In 1913 the emperor Franz Joseph made his father a noble, so the son later wrote his name John von Neumann. At six, his family said, he joked with his father in ancient Greek and divided eight-digit numbers in his head.

pages.t: The boy who read world history
pages.x: As a boy he read all 46 volumes of a German history of the world, and could still recite pages of it decades later. At Princeton he startled historians with what he knew of the Byzantine Empire, and friends found he could repeat books he had read years before, word for word.

At school his tutor Gábor Szegő, later a famous mathematician himself, came home from their first lesson with tears in his eyes at the boy's gift. His father wanted a safe career, so from 1921 he studied chemistry in Berlin and Zurich, and at the same time earned a mathematics doctorate in Budapest. He finished both in 1926, aged 22.
pages.cap: ETH Zurich, where he trained as a chemist

pages.x: In 1926 he went to Göttingen to work with David Hilbert, the leading mathematician of the age, just as quantum physics was being born, and then became the youngest lecturer Berlin had ever had. His book of 1932 gave the new, strange physics of atoms the firm mathematical ground it still stands on.
pages.cap: David Hilbert, his mentor at Göttingen

pages.x: In 1928 he proved that in any game for two where one side's gain is the other's loss, each player has a best strategy, which may mean bluffing at random, as in poker. In 1944, with the economist Oskar Morgenstern, he built on it a theory of economics.
pages.fx: Game theory became a tool of economists, of Cold War nuclear strategy, of biologists studying evolution, and of the design of auctions and of computer programs that play.
pages.cap: Poker, where the best play includes bluffing

pages.x: From 1930 he taught at Princeton, and in 1933, as Hitler took power and Jewish scholars lost their posts in Germany, he became one of the first professors of the new Institute for Advanced Study, beside Einstein. He wore a banker's three-piece suit everywhere, threw famous parties, played loud German marches in his office, and crashed car after car.
pages.cap: Einstein, his colleague at the Institute

pages.x: Two trains 20 miles apart head for each other at 10 mph; a fly zips between them at 15 mph until they meet. How far does it fly? The trick is that the trains meet in an hour, so 15 miles. Von Neumann answered at once. Told that most people try to add up every leg of the trip, he looked puzzled: "What trick? I summed the series."
At Los Alamos he helped solve the hardest problem of the Manhattan Project: how to squeeze a ball of plutonium evenly from all sides, with carefully shaped explosives, until it explodes.
pages.fx: The design worked at the Trinity test, which he watched in July 1945, and destroyed Nagasaki weeks later. Nearly every nuclear weapon since has been built on it.

pages.x: In 1945, drawing on talks with the team that built ENIAC, he wrote the report that described a computer which keeps its program in its memory, beside its data, so a new task needs no rewiring.
pages.fx: Almost every computer and phone since works this way, the "von Neumann architecture". His IAS machine at Princeton was copied around the world, and his team made the first computer weather forecast in 1950.
pages.cap: With the IAS machine at Princeton

pages.x: After the war he feared the Soviet Union, urged the building of the hydrogen bomb and pushed for long-range missiles. In 1955 he joined the Atomic Energy Commission in Washington. In spare hours he imagined machines that could build copies of themselves, and with Stanisław Ulam invented the Monte Carlo method of solving problems with random numbers.
pages.cap: Ivy Mike, the first hydrogen bomb, in 1952

pages.x: In 1955 he was found to have cancer, perhaps from the radiation of the bomb tests he had watched. In 1956 President Eisenhower gave him the Medal of Freedom as he sat in a wheelchair. In hospital in Washington, soldiers guarded his bed in case he let slip secrets. He died in February 1957, aged 53.
pages.cap: Walter Reed hospital, where he died

pages.x: Von Neumann left his mark on pure mathematics, quantum physics, economics, nuclear weapons and weather forecasting, and above all on computing: the design he described in 1945 runs inside almost every computer and phone today.
pts: Put quantum mechanics on firm mathematical ground
Worked out the implosion design of the atomic bomb
